title: Urban II's call and the First Crusade
subject: histoire
description: In November 1095, at Clermont, Pope Urban II made a call that sent tens of thousands of Europeans toward Jerusalem. The Crusades were born.

hero.hook: A twenty-minute speech, and the West set out for Jerusalem.

blocks.text: In November **1095**, in Auvergne, Pope **Urban II** spoke to a crowd. His call was simple: go free Jerusalem and rescue the Christians of the East. In exchange, the forgiveness of sins.

Nobody yet imagined what that speech would set off. Tens of thousands of men were about to head east. The papacy was inventing a holy war. It would reshape, for centuries, the ties between the Christians of the West (often called Latins), the Byzantine Empire in the East, and the Muslim world.

Since the 7th century, Jerusalem had been under Muslim rule. Christian pilgrims still passed through. Everything changed with the **Seljuk Turks**, a warrior people from Asia. In **1071**, at the [[Battle of Manzikert]] in Asia Minor, they crushed the army of the Byzantine Empire, the Eastern Roman Empire. That opened up Anatolia, the heart of what is now Turkey.

blocks.caption: Manzikert, 1071: Byzantium loses Anatolia to the Seljuks

blocks.text: Cornered, the Byzantine emperor [[Alexios I Komnenos]] asked Rome for help. Yet since the [[Schism of 1054]], the Catholic Church of the West and the Orthodox Church of the East had been separate. For Urban II the moment was perfect: he could assert the pope's authority and turn the violence of the knights toward a cause far from home. The Church had already tried to curb these private wars with the [[Peace of God]], a movement to protect non-combatants.
At Manzikert, Sultan Alp Arslan captured the Byzantine emperor. Instead of killing him, he treated him with honor and then set him free.

On **November 27, 1095**, at the [[Council of Clermont]], a great Church assembly, Urban II promised a [[Plenary indulgence]] to everyone who left: the full remission of the penalties owed for sin. The expedition became an armed pilgrimage. The cry **“God wills it!”** spread. Volunteers sewed a red cross onto their shoulder: they “took the cross.”

blocks.caption: The Council of Clermont, 1095: the call that launched the First Crusade

blocks.text: The fervor quickly slipped out of the pope's hands. Before the lords set out, [[Peter the Hermit]], a popular preacher, led a crowd of poor people east. With no discipline and no supplies, this “Crusade of the Poor” looted its way across Europe and was wiped out in Anatolia. Zeal alone does not make an army.

In **1096** the barons' crusade set out: **Godfrey of Bouillon**, a lord from Lorraine, [[Bohemond of Taranto]], a Norman prince from southern Italy, and other leaders. Alexios demanded oaths from them. After the long siege of **Antioch** (1097-1098), a great city in Syria, the survivors reached Jerusalem. On **July 15, 1099**, the city fell. The massacre marked Muslim memory for centuries.

Godfrey of Bouillon refused the title of king. He had himself called [[Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre]], protector of the tomb of Christ: too humble, he said, to wear a crown of gold where Christ had worn thorns.

The crusaders founded the [[Crusader States]], four small Christian states in the Near East. Later the [[Templars]], warrior monks, protected the pilgrims. In **1187**, [[Saladin]], a Muslim sultan, took Jerusalem back. Other crusades followed, until the fall of Acre, the last Latin stronghold, in **1291**.

blocks.text: Militarily, the adventure ended badly. Culturally, it still brought East and West closer: Greek science passed on by Arab scholars, new techniques, new goods, the banking methods of the military orders. Europe learned to mobilize under one banner.

The legacy stays ambiguous. Urban II's call forged a shared Christian identity in the West. It also dug a lasting mistrust between religions. A speech of a few minutes opened two centuries of war and exchange.

In **1095**, Urban II turned a Byzantine request for help into an armed pilgrimage. In **1099** Jerusalem fell; in **1291** the Latin presence collapsed. The Crusades united the West and divided memories for centuries.
